title: Monolithic high density integrated photonics on bulk lithium niobate
abstract: Functional electro-optic (EO) tunable photonic integrated circuits are crucial to next-generation information processing and advanced computing, where ferroelectric materials such as lithium niobate (LiNbO3) provide outstanding optical properties and versatile tuning mechanisms. However, beyond achieving high-performance devices, practical deployment of LiNbO3 photonic integrated circuits requires rapid and cost-effective scale-up, which remains challenging because of the fabrication complexity and high costs of ion-sliced thin-film lithium niobate and wafer bonding processes. To address this gap, we demonstrate a fully monolithic photonic platform, amorphous silicon carbide (a-SiC) on bulk LiNbO3 crystal substrate, enabling scalable, CMOS-compatible, low-cost, and high-density photonic integrated circuits without relying on thin-film LiNbO3. This integration approach breaks the long-standing cost-performance-scalability tradeoff, and intrinsically eliminates the need for sophisticated fabrication processes, including ion slicing, wafer bonding, and LiNbO3 etching. It realizes high-density, low-loss, and record high EO tuning efficiency of VpiL = 2.87 Vcm on bulk LiNbO3 crystal substrate. Furthermore, leveraging slow-light effect near photonic crystal bandgap, an 8.5-fold EO tuning efficiency enhancement is achieved, highlighting the platform's capability in confinement control and dispersion engineering.
one_liner: Monolithic a-SiC-on-bulk-LiNbO3 enables dense, low-loss EO photonic circuits without thin-film LN processing.
why_it_matters: It offers a lower-cost route to scalable lithium-niobate photonics while retaining strong electro-optic tuning for integrated information processors.
detailed_summary: The work demonstrates amorphous silicon carbide photonics fabricated directly on bulk lithium niobate, avoiding ion slicing, wafer bonding, and LiNbO3 etching. The platform achieves high-density, low-loss electro-optic circuits with VpiL = 2.87 Vcm. By exploiting slow light near a photonic-crystal bandgap, the authors further enhance EO tuning efficiency by 8.5x.
main_result: A fully monolithic bulk-LiNbO3 photonic platform delivers record EO tuning efficiency and slow-light-enhanced modulation.
application_angle: The approach targets manufacturable, lower-cost EO photonic integrated circuits for computing, signal processing, and scalable photonic systems.

title: Resolving and resetting the charge environment of single T-centers in silicon p-i-n waveguides
abstract: The silicon T-center is a telecom-band spin-photon interface in a manufacturable photonics platform. In nanophotonic devices, however, its optical linewidth is broadened by a fluctuating charge environment, limiting photon indistinguishability for quantum networking. Here, we address this challenge through characterization and suppression of the local charge-noise of single T-centers in lateral p-i-n waveguides, demonstrating an unheralded method of T-center optical linewidth narrowing. Above-band illumination resets the charge environment, neutralizing the local field and suppressing spectral diffusion. Across 46 emitters this reset narrows the median linewidth 3.5-fold to 0.57(11) GHz, and an optimized emitter reaches 128(22) MHz, the narrowest unheralded linewidth reported for an integrated T-center. The narrowed transition supports coherent optical Rabi oscillations with a coherence time of 20(2) ns. Finally, we perform Stark-shift tuning using the p-i-n junction, and read out the local electric field and the charge-noise width at 15 mK. An analytical model of proximal surfaces, bulk, and junction field effects provides good agreement with our findings. Our multi-pronged characterization of the nanophotonic-integrated T-center charge environment enables future device optimization toward scalable quantum interconnects.
one_liner: Above-band illumination resets charge noise around single silicon T-centers, narrowing telecom optical linewidths in p-i-n waveguides.
why_it_matters: Reducing spectral diffusion in integrated T-centers directly improves photon indistinguishability for silicon quantum-network nodes.
detailed_summary: The paper characterizes and suppresses local charge noise for single T-centers embedded in lateral silicon p-i-n waveguides at cryogenic temperature. Above-band illumination resets the charge environment, reducing median linewidth by 3.5x to 0.57(11) GHz across 46 emitters, with a best unheralded linewidth of 128(22) MHz. The narrowed transition supports coherent optical Rabi oscillations with 20(2) ns coherence, and p-i-n Stark tuning is used to read out local fields and charge-noise widths.
platform_or_system: single T-centers in silicon p-i-n waveguides
main_result: The authors demonstrate unheralded linewidth narrowing, coherent optical control, Stark tuning, and charge-field diagnostics for integrated T-centers.
application_angle: This is a practical device-engineering step toward scalable silicon spin-photon interfaces for quantum interconnects and telecom quantum networks.

title: zenDot: An LLM-integrated quantum TCAD platform for semiconductor quantum-device design and optimization automation
abstract: Semiconductor quantum-device design still lacks an integrated Technology Computer-Aided Design (TCAD)-like environment that connects material geometry, quantum many-body simulation, and automated design. Here we introduce zenDot, a large-language model (LLM)-integrated quantum TCAD platform that links a material-labelled device state to a unified condensed-matter physics toolbox. The device and calculation components are integrated into a desktop workbench, Python API, and an embedded LLM agent, allowing electrostatics, charge and transport characterization, correlated-state calculations, and qubit modelling to be executed within one reproducible environment. We demonstrate zenDot on a Si/SiO2 double quantum dot, where a single device state reproduces the characterization workflow and supports hybrid, tunnel-charge, and singlet-triplet qubit analyses. A platform-level universal-control scan revises the singlet-triplet operating point and reduces the predicted worst-gate infidelity by nearly 30-fold. Beyond analysis, the LLM agent directly operates the same physics environment as human users, proposing design changes, executing registered simulations, and iterating on solver-returned metrics under physics-aware validation. Across three demonstration tasks it completes 18 validated design iterations, including geometry modification followed by a full re-solve from the material stack. zenDot establishes a machine-operable quantum TCAD workflow that connects device physics with LLM-driven design exploration.
one_liner: zenDot integrates quantum-device TCAD, many-body simulation, qubit modeling, and an LLM agent for automated semiconductor design.
why_it_matters: It points toward reproducible, machine-operable workflows for optimizing semiconductor quantum devices beyond manual simulation loops.
detailed_summary: zenDot links material-labeled device states to electrostatics, transport, correlated-state calculations, and qubit modeling through a desktop workbench, Python API, and embedded LLM agent. A Si/SiO2 double quantum dot example supports hybrid, tunnel-charge, and singlet-triplet qubit analyses from one reproducible state. A universal-control scan revises the singlet-triplet operating point and reduces predicted worst-gate infidelity by nearly 30x, while the LLM completes 18 validated design iterations across three tasks.
platform_or_system: Si/SiO2 semiconductor double quantum dot TCAD
main_result: The platform demonstrates closed-loop, physics-validated quantum-device design iterations including geometry changes and full re-solves.
application_angle: Automated quantum TCAD could accelerate semiconductor qubit optimization and make device-design workflows more reproducible.

title: Quantum Rabi oscillations of a qubit strongly coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide
abstract: We theoretically investigate quantum Rabi oscillations in a system consisting of a two-level atom (qubit) strongly coupled to a one-dimensional open waveguide. In contrast to conventional cavity quantum electrodynamics, the qubit interacts with a continuum of propagating modes, which gives rise to fundamentally different dynamical behavior. Within the rotating-wave approximation, we express the multimode Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian in terms of collective bosonic operators and show that the system possesses two integrals of motion, enabling an exact diagonalization of the Hamiltonian in the single-excitation subspace. Considering the initially excited qubit and field states described by multiphoton Fock-like states, we demonstrate that the Rabi oscillations represent a collective phenomenon corresponding to oscillations between multiphoton states differing by a single photon. We then extend our analysis to multiphoton processes in which the initial field is a multimode coherent state in a continuous spectrum. In this case, the Rabi frequency is shown to be sensitive to the spectral profile of the function that generates the coherent state.
one_liner: A theory study derives collective quantum Rabi oscillations for a qubit strongly coupled to a continuum 1D waveguide.
why_it_matters: It clarifies strong-coupling dynamics outside cavities, relevant to waveguide-QED architectures for photonic quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The authors analyze a two-level qubit strongly coupled to an open one-dimensional waveguide, where the field is a continuum rather than a discrete cavity mode. Within the rotating-wave approximation, they reformulate the multimode Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian using collective bosonic operators and identify two integrals of motion enabling exact single-excitation diagonalization. The resulting Rabi oscillations are collective transitions between multiphoton states, with coherent-state Rabi frequencies depending on the spectral profile.
platform_or_system: qubit strongly coupled to a 1D waveguide
main_result: The work provides an exact theoretical description of collective Rabi oscillations in continuum waveguide-QED settings.
application_angle: The model informs design and interpretation of waveguide-based quantum emitters, routers, and integrated photonic quantum interfaces.

title: Nanocavity Confinement by Orthogonal Valley- and SSH- Topological Interfaces In Glide-Symmetric Photonic Crystal Structures
abstract: Valley photonic crystals enable valley-dependent transport and chirality-selective emission, but incorporating wavelength-scale localization remains challenging. Existing valley-photonic-crystal cavities rely on finite defects or local lattice modifications that require structure-specific optimization and offer limited continuous control. Here, we theoretically and experimentally demonstrate two-dimensional nanocavity confinement using two orthogonal domain walls in a glide-symmetric valley photonic crystal. A valley domain wall confines the guided interface mode transversely, while an SSH-like domain wall localizes it longitudinally. Starting from a glide-symmetry-protected Dirac point in a bearded-interface waveguide, controlled displacements of adjacent triangular holes open a topological gap in the continuous guided-mode dispersion. The displacement amplitude $ΔR$ tunes the gap, mode volume, and intrinsic radiative $Q$ factor. Implemented in a silicon photonic-crystal slab, the structure exhibits localized resonances within the topological mode gap and systematic spectral tuning with $ΔR$. The maximum measured loaded $Q$ factor is $1.2\times10^{4}$. This approach enables continuously tunable, high-$Q$ nanocavities integrated into topological waveguide networks for compact resonant devices and enhanced light--matter interactions.
one_liner: Orthogonal valley and SSH topological domain walls create tunable high-Q nanocavities in glide-symmetric photonic crystals.
why_it_matters: The method adds wavelength-scale localization to topological photonic networks with continuous control over resonance properties.
detailed_summary: The paper demonstrates two-dimensional nanocavity confinement using a transverse valley domain wall and a longitudinal SSH-like domain wall in a glide-symmetric photonic crystal. Controlled displacement of triangular holes opens a tunable topological gap in the guided-mode dispersion. Silicon slab devices show localized resonances inside the gap, systematic spectral tuning with displacement amplitude, and a maximum measured loaded Q of 1.2e4.
main_result: The authors experimentally realize continuously tunable topological nanocavities with measured loaded Q up to 1.2e4.
application_angle: Such cavities can support compact resonant devices and enhanced light-matter interaction inside robust topological waveguide networks.

title: Controlling rotations of magnetically levitated superconductors
abstract: Magnetically trapped type-I superconductors are promising candidates for precision experiments at the quantum-to-classical borderline, with applications in quantum sensing of forces and accelerations and fundamental tests of quantum physics. Here, we show how the rotational motion of micron-sized superconductors is strongly affected by (i) the diamagnetic torques due to the gradient of the trapping field and by (ii) the gyromagnetic coupling due to Einstein-de Haas and Barnett effects. We show that this allows the three-dimensional alignment of asperhical superconductors in the trap center, as required for future sensing applications and quantum experiments, and determine the resulting librational trapping frequencies. Finally, we propose an experiment to probe gyromagnetic coupling in levitated superconductors and we discuss how it can be used to control the particle rotation.
one_liner: A theory proposal shows how diamagnetic torques and gyromagnetic coupling control rotations of levitated type-I superconductors.
why_it_matters: Rotational alignment and control are key requirements for using levitated superconductors as precision force and acceleration sensors.
detailed_summary: The work studies rotational dynamics of micron-scale type-I superconductors in magnetic traps. It shows that field-gradient-induced diamagnetic torques and gyromagnetic coupling from Einstein-de Haas and Barnett effects can align aspherical particles in three dimensions. The authors estimate librational trapping frequencies and propose an experiment to probe and exploit gyromagnetic coupling for rotation control.
main_result: The paper establishes mechanisms and experimental routes for three-dimensional rotational alignment of levitated superconducting particles.
application_angle: Controlled rotations would improve levitated-superconductor platforms for precision inertial sensing and tests of mesoscopic quantum physics.

title: Quantum Mpemba Speedups in the Thermodynamics of Landauer Erasure
abstract: We investigate how nonequilibrium quantum initial states can reduce the finite-time thermodynamic cost of Landauer erasure. Considering a general finite-dimensional quantum memory coupled to a thermal reservoir via a Davies generator, we show that the dissipated heat at a fixed operational erasure fidelity is largely controlled by the overlap of the initial state with the slowest Liouvillian relaxation mode. We derive a modified finite-time Landauer bound in which the excess dissipation above the quasistatic limit scales quadratically with this slow mode projection, and we prove a sufficient Mpemba Landauer condition under which a hotter state can erase faster and dissipate less heat than a colder preparation, without violating Landauer's principle. A minimal qutrit model illustrates these quantum Mpemba speedups and reveals broad parameter regimes where coherence and Hamiltonian-induced modes conspire to suppress finite-time entropy production. We further identify practical control knobs, including temperature tuning, coherence engineering, and Hamiltonian shaping of Liouvillian spectra, which enable Mpemba-enhanced erasure to be directly tested on platforms such as superconducting circuits, trapped ions, semiconductor quantum dots, and solid-state spins.
one_liner: Shows how quantum Mpemba effects can reduce finite-time heat dissipation in Landauer erasure of quantum memories.
why_it_matters: It connects nonequilibrium state preparation to lower erasure cost, giving testable control knobs for superconducting, ion, dot, and spin hardware.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes finite-dimensional quantum memories coupled to a thermal bath through a Davies generator and identifies the slowest Liouvillian mode projection as a key predictor of finite-time erasure cost. It derives a modified Landauer bound where excess dissipation scales quadratically with this projection. A qutrit model shows regimes where hotter or more coherent initial states erase faster and with less heat than colder preparations, consistent with Landauer's principle.
main_result: A finite-time Landauer bound and sufficient Mpemba condition are derived for quantum erasure with suppressed dissipation.
application_angle: The proposed knobs, including temperature tuning, coherence engineering, and Hamiltonian shaping, map onto realistic quantum processors and solid-state platforms.

title: Optimal bounds on the classical value of the repeated CHSH game
abstract: We show that the maximum winning probability in the repeated CHSH game for classical strategies is at most $\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{4}\right)^n$. Together with a matching lower bound by Barak et al. (FOCS'2008), this determines the asymptotic value of the repeated CHSH game exactly. We also show that, if an XOR game has a gap between classical and quantum values, there is also a gap between the asymptotic values for the repeated game.
one_liner: Determines the exact asymptotic classical value of the repeated CHSH game.
why_it_matters: Sharper repeated-game bounds strengthen the theoretical baseline for Bell-test amplification and device-independent quantum advantage claims.
detailed_summary: The work proves that the optimal classical winning probability for n repeated CHSH games is at most ((1+sqrt(5))/4)^n. Together with a known matching construction, this fixes the asymptotic value exactly. It also shows that any XOR game with a quantum-classical value gap retains a gap at the repeated-game asymptotic level.
main_result: The asymptotic classical value of repeated CHSH is proven exactly with a matching upper and lower bound.
application_angle: The result improves the certification framework behind photonic Bell tests, randomness expansion, and device-independent protocols.

title: Raman-detected quantum dot microscopy for nanoscale electrostatic potential imaging
abstract: Quantification of electrostatic potentials at the nanoscale is crucial for understanding the principles governing properties of materials across multiple length scales. Currently, one of the most successful approaches relies on the charging response of a molecular quantum dot, suspended on a tip of a scanning probe microscope and measured using dynamic force spectroscopy. We investigate the possibility of an optical detection, aiming to improve the speed and reduce the complexity of this measurement scheme. We show that the integrated tip-enhanced Raman scattering intensity strongly correlates with the charge state of the quantum dot, and use it to map the electrostatic potential of a single atom. A quantitative equivalence with the established force spectroscopy method is found. We address the underlying photophysical principle of this new method by measuring the Raman spectra as a function of excitation wavelength and the molecular quantum dot charge. We reveal that the observed Raman intensity variations are primarily driven by transitions between resonant and non-resonant Raman scattering regimes of the molecule.
one_liner: Demonstrates Raman-readout quantum dot microscopy for nanoscale electrostatic potential imaging down to a single atom.
why_it_matters: Optical charge-state readout could make scanning-probe potential mapping faster and less mechanically complex than force-spectroscopy approaches.
detailed_summary: The authors use integrated tip-enhanced Raman scattering intensity as an optical proxy for the charge state of a molecular quantum dot on a scanning probe tip. They map the electrostatic potential of a single atom and find quantitative equivalence with established dynamic force spectroscopy. Wavelength- and charge-dependent spectra indicate that Raman intensity changes arise mainly from switching between resonant and non-resonant Raman regimes.
main_result: Raman intensity is shown to quantitatively report quantum-dot charge state and nanoscale electrostatic potential.
application_angle: The method points toward faster nanoscale electrostatic imaging for materials, surfaces, and atomic-scale device characterization.

title: Quantum gate lower bounds for loss-tolerant position verification
abstract: Quantum position-verification is a cryptographic task wherein a verifier attempts to establish the location in space of a prover. Recent experiments have implemented a well-studied class of position-verification schemes, known as the $f$-BB84 scenario, but their security under realistic loss and imperfect state preparation remains incompletely understood. We give a new lower bound on any attack on this scheme, in particular proving nearly-linear quantum gate lower bounds on the attacker, even when allowing the attacker to declare a transmission loss of up to $50\%$, allowing for the challenges prepared by the referee to be imperfect, and allowing the quantum messages used in the protocol to be arbitrarily slow. Our results are applicable to recent and upcoming experimental implementations of $f$-BB84, and in particular establish their security under a bounded quantum gate assumption on the attacker. The key ingredient is a tight analytic tradeoff for a lossy BB84 monogamy-of-entanglement game, valid without requiring the attackers' outputs to agree, which replaces observations previously made numerically.
one_liner: Proves nearly linear quantum-gate lower bounds for attacks on lossy f-BB84 position-verification protocols.
why_it_matters: It gives experimentally relevant security evidence for position verification even with loss, imperfect preparation, and slow quantum messages.
detailed_summary: The paper studies quantum position verification in the f-BB84 scenario under realistic imperfections. It proves nearly linear quantum gate lower bounds for attackers even when up to 50 percent loss is declared, prepared states are imperfect, and quantum messages are arbitrarily slow. The proof uses a tight analytic tradeoff for a lossy BB84 monogamy-of-entanglement game without requiring attacker output agreement.
main_result: Attacks on realistic f-BB84 position verification require nearly linear quantum gate complexity under bounded-quantum-computation assumptions.
application_angle: The bounds support practical security claims for recent and upcoming quantum position-verification experiments.

title: MoMPy: automated construction of moment matrices for semidefinite programming relaxations
abstract: We present MoMPy, an open-source Python package that provides a unified, declarative construction of moment matrices for semidefinite programming (SDP) hierarchies. The user declares operator labels together with a small set of structural relations, and MoMPy returns a matrix of SDP variable indices in which every implied identification has already been made, ready for CVXPY or any other modelling layer. Internally, the identification problem is recast as a word-rewriting problem on tuples of integers and solved with a memoised breadth-first closure coupled to a disjoint-set forest, so that each distinct monomial is processed exactly once per build, however many matrix entries it eventually labels. The central abstraction is independent of the physical scenario: the same construction handles tracial, state (NPA), and block-valued moments, with no notion of parties, settings or preparations. We demonstrate this generality on a tripartite Mermin inequality, the bipartite CHSH inequality, measurement compatibility in a steering scenario, state discrimination and dimension witnessing in prepare-and-measure scenarios, device-independent randomness certification, and certification of deterministic correlations from known ensembles. The construction is validated against an independent brute-force implementation and benchmarked across eight structurally distinct scenarios, spanning bipartite and tripartite Bell tests, heterogeneous-outcome, steering-type, jointly-measurable and network configurations.
one_liner: Introduces MoMPy, a Python tool for declarative construction of SDP moment matrices across quantum-information scenarios.
why_it_matters: It lowers the implementation barrier for Bell, steering, randomness, and prepare-and-measure certification workflows using SDP hierarchies.
detailed_summary: MoMPy lets users declare operator labels and structural relations, then returns moment-matrix SDP variable indices with implied identifications already resolved. The implementation recasts identifications as word rewriting and uses memoized closure with a disjoint-set forest. It supports tracial, state, and block-valued moments and is validated across Bell, steering, compatibility, discrimination, dimension-witnessing, and randomness-certification examples.
main_result: An open-source package automates reusable, scenario-independent construction of moment matrices for SDP relaxations.
application_angle: The package can speed analysis pipelines for photonic nonlocality experiments and device-independent certification.

title: Non-invertible Lattice 1-Form Symmetries for Non-Abelian Topological Order
abstract: Higher-form symmetries generalize conventional global symmetries and act on lower-dimensional submanifolds of a quantum system. While Abelian topological phases can be organized by 1-form symmetries that form a group, non-Abelian topological phases based on finite groups require 1-form symmetry operators governed by non-invertible fusion algebras. In this work, we make this statement precise in quantum double lattice models $\mathcal D(G)$ for finite non-Abelian groups $G$. We construct the electric, magnetic, and dyonic 1-form operators directly at the lattice fixed point and show that together they form a complete nonlocal diagnostic algebra for the topological Hilbert space. Using these operators, we explicitly determine the cylinder and torus ground-state subspaces for arbitrary finite $G$. Furthermore, we calculate the microscopic fusion and gluing of the 1-form symmetries and show that their topological deformation properties emerge after projection to the defect-free topological subspace. Our results establish ground states of non-Abelian quantum double models as a concrete microscopic realization of spontaneous non-invertible 1-form symmetry breaking and provide an operator language that may be useful for characterizing such states in quantum processors.
one_liner: Builds lattice 1-form symmetry operators for non-Abelian quantum double models and their non-invertible fusion algebra.
why_it_matters: It gives a microscopic operator language for diagnosing non-Abelian topological order relevant to topological quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The authors construct electric, magnetic, and dyonic 1-form operators directly in finite-group non-Abelian quantum double lattice models. These operators form a diagnostic algebra for the topological Hilbert space and allow explicit determination of cylinder and torus ground-state subspaces. The work also computes microscopic fusion and gluing, showing how topological deformation properties emerge after projection to the defect-free subspace.
main_result: Non-Abelian quantum double ground states are characterized as microscopic realizations of spontaneous non-invertible 1-form symmetry breaking.
application_angle: The operator framework may help characterize and benchmark non-Abelian topological states in quantum simulators and processors.

title: Spectral filtering and crystal length as control parameters for conditional correlations in quantum imaging
abstract: We establish spectral filtering as a control parameter for the conditional momentum and position correlations of SPDC biphotons used in quantum imaging. The conditional momentum uncertainty in spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) is strongly crystal-length and spectral-filter dependent along the walk-off axis; therefore, the effect is observed only in critically phase-matched (CPM) crystals such as $β$-barium borate (BBO) crystals, while quasi-phase-matched (QPM) crystals and the non-walk-off axis of BBO remain scaled strictly according to the standard pump waist size ($w_0$) dependent scaling law $1/w_0$-independent of the filter. In position space, the spectral-filter effect is universal and produces a flat-dip-rise (FDR) profile in every crystal class examined. Although this FDR profile was previously demonstrated in BBO only in the nondegenerate regime, our results establish its generality: the FDR dip is also present at exact degeneracy in QPM crystals, an unexpected feature that was previously thought to deliver a resolution advantage in the nondegenerate regime alone. Our treatment applies to all SPDC-based quantum-imaging regimes (including CPM and QPM crystals, walk-off and non-walk-off axes, degenerate and nondegenerate emission, and signal and idler filtering) and offers enhanced quantum-imaging resolution via the design rules presented-most prominently along the walk-off axis of CPM crystals (in far field) and across all transverse axes in the near field.
one_liner: Spectral filtering and SPDC crystal length are shown to tune conditional correlations for quantum-imaging resolution.
why_it_matters: It turns filter bandwidth and crystal geometry into practical design knobs for near- and far-field SPDC quantum imaging.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes how spectral filtering modifies conditional momentum and position correlations of SPDC biphotons across CPM and QPM crystals. Along the BBO walk-off axis, far-field momentum uncertainty depends strongly on crystal length and filter bandwidth, while QPM and non-walk-off axes follow the usual pump-waist scaling. In position space, the filter effect is universal and produces a flat-dip-rise profile, including at exact degeneracy in QPM crystals.
main_result: The work establishes spectral filtering and crystal length as control parameters for conditional SPDC correlations across imaging regimes.
application_angle: The design rules can improve spatial resolution in SPDC-based quantum imaging by choosing filter bandwidth, crystal class, and geometry deliberately.

title: Two-Photon Bound States in the Continuum: A No-Go Theorem and Long-Lived Quasi-Bound States
abstract: Two-photon bound states in the continuum provide a stringent setting in which quantum interference must suppress radiative decay despite photon--photon interactions. Here, we prove a no-go theorem showing that a single nonlinear mode linearly coupled to a noninteracting bosonic continuum cannot support an interaction-active two-photon bound state in the continuum, provided the local spectral density vanishes only at isolated energies. Apart from this regularity condition, the result is independent of the continuum dispersion and the frequency-dependent coupling. Although such an exact bound state is forbidden, long-lived two-photon quasi-bound states remain possible. For a giant Kerr cavity nonlocally coupled to a waveguide, we derive the asymptotic scaling of the two-photon decay rate with the coupling-point separation from weak nonlinearity to the hard-core limit. We further identify a regime in which the two-photon resonance is substantially longer lived than the single-photon excitation. Our work establishes the limits of exact multiphoton confinement while opening a route to engineering long-lived interacting few-photon states.
one_liner: A no-go theorem rules out exact interaction-active two-photon BICs in a broad single-mode nonlinear waveguide setting.
why_it_matters: It clarifies what few-photon confinement schemes cannot achieve, while identifying routes to long-lived interacting photon resonances.
detailed_summary: The paper proves that a single nonlinear mode linearly coupled to a noninteracting bosonic continuum cannot host an interaction-active two-photon bound state in the continuum when the local spectral density only vanishes at isolated energies. The result is dispersion- and coupling-profile independent under that regularity condition. It then studies a giant Kerr cavity nonlocally coupled to a waveguide and derives scaling laws for long-lived two-photon quasi-bound-state decay.
platform_or_system: Giant Kerr cavity coupled to a waveguide
main_result: Exact interaction-active two-photon BICs are forbidden in the stated model, but parametrically long-lived two-photon quasi-bound states can be engineered.
application_angle: The results guide realistic designs for few-photon nonlinear photonic memories, gates, and waveguide-QED devices.

title: Imaginary Barrier, Real Transfer: Non-Hermitian Dynamical Tunnelling
abstract: We identify a non-Hermitian counterpart of dynamical tunnelling induced by a localised absorbing region in a symmetric confining potential. The absorbing region, described by an imaginary potential barrier, induces an effective double-well structure with a pair of long-lived states that have little population in the barrier. In contrast to the periodic tunnel oscillations through a real barrier, the system slowly evolves towards equal population of the two sides, while the absorbing region remains only weakly populated. We demonstrate this generic mechanism in two continuous potentials, and capture its essence analytically in a minimal $3\times 3$ matrix model. We propose a realistic optical waveguide setup for the experimental observation of the effect.
one_liner: A localized absorber can induce non-Hermitian dynamical tunnelling with weak barrier population and long-lived states.
why_it_matters: It proposes an optical-waveguide route to observe tunnelling-like transfer driven by loss rather than a real potential barrier.
detailed_summary: The paper identifies a non-Hermitian analogue of dynamical tunnelling caused by a localized imaginary potential barrier in a symmetric confining potential. The absorber creates an effective double-well structure with long-lived states that avoid the lossy region. Instead of coherent oscillations through a real barrier, the system relaxes slowly toward equal left-right population while keeping the absorbing region weakly occupied.
main_result: The authors demonstrate and model non-Hermitian dynamical tunnelling induced by a localized absorber.
application_angle: The proposed waveguide implementation could enable controlled light transfer and state shaping using engineered loss profiles.

title: Sensitivity Scaling and Limits of Cavity Enhancement in Miniaturized Optically Pumped Magnetometers
abstract: The sensitivity of miniaturized optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs) is limited by weak atom-light coupling, which an optical cavity can enhance. In this work, we model the photon-shot-noise-limited sensitivity of cavity-enhanced OPMs in the regime of strongly collisionally broadened optical transitions, characteristic of buffer-gas-filled miniaturized vapor cells. The cavity enhancement is benchmarked against a single-pass free-induction-decay OPM employing Faraday-rotation readout, with the probe power and detuning jointly optimized using the Cramér-Rao lower bound as a figure of merit. For a Fabry-Pérot cavity, we compare side-of-fringe, homodyne, Pound-Drever-Hall, and Faraday-rotation readout. All four yield an optimal sensitivity enhancement scaling as $α\sqrt{2\mathcal{F}/π}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the cavity finesse and $0.5\leq α\leq 1$ is a readout-dependent prefactor. The enhancement is maximized at critical coupling, and we quantify its degradation away from this point. We further show that, despite spin-dependent absorption associated with the ensemble's vector polarizability, near-critical coupling can be maintained throughout spin precession at arbitrary finesse by exceeding a derived probe-power threshold and increasing the atomic detuning with finesse. We also establish a limit to the maximum cavity enhancement set by vector light-shift noise.
one_liner: Cavity-enhanced miniaturized OPMs gain sensitivity as roughly alpha sqrt(2F/pi) until vector light-shift noise limits them.
why_it_matters: It gives quantitative design limits for compact high-sensitivity magnetometers using realistic buffer-gas vapor cells.
detailed_summary: The paper models photon-shot-noise-limited sensitivity in cavity-enhanced miniaturized optically pumped magnetometers with strongly collisionally broadened transitions. It benchmarks multiple Fabry-Perot readouts, including side-of-fringe, homodyne, Pound-Drever-Hall, and Faraday rotation, against optimized single-pass free-induction readout. The optimal enhancement scales as alpha sqrt(2F/pi), is maximized near critical coupling, and is ultimately capped by vector light-shift noise.
main_result: The work derives sensitivity scaling, critical-coupling requirements, and light-shift-noise limits for miniaturized cavity-enhanced OPMs.
application_angle: These results support engineering compact magnetometers for biomagnetism, navigation, and field sensing where size and optical depth are constrained.

title: Time-optimal quantum gates with bang-bang control in multilevel systems
abstract: We determine the optimal quantum manipulation protocols for implementing high-fidelity, fast single-qubit gates. We demonstrate that the time-optimal pulse sequence is a ``bang-bang'' sequence: discrete pulses of either positive or negative maximum amplitude or zero. The non-adiabatic bang-bang pulse sequence minimizes gate duration providing a speedup for low-frequency architectures. We first derive the protocol for a transversally driven two-level system, extracting exact analytic expressions for minimum gate times. We then extend this framework to general multilevel architectures, identifying conditions that enable the coherent suppression of leakage errors. Using the fluxonium circuit as a representative case study, we optimize $X/2$ and $Y/2$ gates through a combination of discrete bang sequences and continuous waveform smoothing. This approach preserves near-optimal execution speeds while mitigating transitions outside the computational subspace. Open-system simulations demonstrate that these sequences outperform commensurate and resonant pulse schemes across different fluxonium regimes, achieving low-error manipulation significantly faster than standard resonant control, even in the presence of $1/f$ flux noise and dissipation.
one_liner: Time-optimal single-qubit gates in multilevel devices emerge as bang-bang pulses with leakage-aware smoothing.
why_it_matters: It offers faster high-fidelity control for low-frequency qubit architectures such as fluxonium under realistic noise and leakage constraints.
detailed_summary: The paper derives time-optimal protocols for single-qubit gates, showing that optimal control uses discrete positive, negative, or zero-amplitude bang-bang segments. It extends the framework from two-level systems to multilevel architectures and identifies conditions for coherent leakage suppression. For fluxonium, optimized X/2 and Y/2 gates combine discrete bang sequences with waveform smoothing and outperform resonant or commensurate schemes in open-system simulations.
main_result: Bang-bang-based protocols achieve near-optimal fast single-qubit gates with reduced leakage and lower simulated error than standard resonant control.
application_angle: The method can shorten gate times in superconducting hardware while maintaining fidelity in the presence of dissipation and flux noise.

title: Engineering two-qubit gates via anisotropic exchange in germanium spin qubits
abstract: Germanium hole spin qubits are a promising and versatile platform for quantum computation and simulation. In this system, strong spin-orbit interaction (SOI) renders the single-qubit $g$-tensor anisotropic and electrically tunable, enabling operational sweet spots with reduced noise sensitivity. SOI also transforms the isotropic two-qubit exchange coupling into an anisotropic tensor whose geometry is inherited from the single-qubit $g$-tensors and spin-flip tunnelling. Here, using two hole spin qubits in a strained-germanium quantum well and full vector control of the magnetic field, we map this exchange tensor, separate it into longitudinal and transverse components, and show that they govern controlled-phase and SWAP-like dynamics, respectively. We find that the longitudinal exchange can be tuned via the magnetic field orientation from a conventional positive value, through zero, to an effectively negative one, as measured by inverted exchange-split spin transitions. The magnetic field direction thus provides continuous control over the interaction Hamiltonian: at a point of purely transverse exchange, we engineer a single-pulse baseband iSWAP, unattainable under isotropic exchange. Linking $g$-tensor geometry to exchange anisotropy establishes native Hamiltonian engineering, enabling spin-based quantum simulation and gate sets selected by the global field orientation alone.
one_liner: Germanium hole spin qubits use magnetic-field orientation to tune anisotropic exchange from CZ-like to iSWAP-like dynamics.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates native Hamiltonian engineering in a scalable semiconductor spin-qubit platform using global field direction.
detailed_summary: The paper studies two hole spin qubits in a strained-germanium quantum well, where spin-orbit interaction makes the g-tensor anisotropic and electrically tunable. With vector magnetic-field control, it maps the exchange tensor into longitudinal and transverse components tied to controlled-phase and SWAP-like dynamics. The longitudinal exchange is tuned through positive, zero, and effectively negative values, enabling a purely transverse point for a single-pulse baseband iSWAP.
main_result: The authors map and control anisotropic exchange to realize field-orientation-selected two-qubit interaction Hamiltonians, including a native iSWAP regime.
application_angle: This enables semiconductor spin-qubit gate sets and quantum-simulation interactions selected by magnetic-field geometry rather than local pulse complexity.

title: Parallel Spatial Photonic Programming of Optoelectronic IGZO RRAM with a compact $μ$LED Array
abstract: Optoelectronic resistive random-access memory elements (ORRAM) are critical emerging devices that leverage photonic technologies to bring the advantages of optical programming to traditionally electronic memristive platforms for neuromorphic computing and artificial intelligence. In this work, a free-space optic micro-LED ($μ$LED) array is combined with a 2-terminal oxide semiconductor ORRAM (based on IGZO\textsubscript{Rich}/IGZO active layers), to realise parallel spatial programming of form-free memristive arrays. We report the optical and electrical programming of resistive states with potentiation/depression analysis of various stimuli parameters (pulse frequency, pulse width, pulse amplitude). Further, we demonstrate the simultaneous photonic-electronic programming of the ORRAM with optical SET (blue 450\,nm) and electrical RESET functionality. Persistent photocurrent is also observed and exploited as a pathway to fading memory or synaptic plasticity for temporal bit encoding. Finally, parallel optical $μ$LED to ORRAM channels are demonstrated to achieve the simultaneous photonic programming of multiple devices and the writing of spatial patterns across a chip of memristive IGZO devices. This work highlights the light-enabled scalability of the optoelectronic platform and the feasibility of ORRAM to interface with spatially-multiplexed optical sources to bring neuromorphic technologies directly into applications that process and sense in the optical domain.
one_liner: A compact micro-LED array optically programs IGZO optoelectronic RRAM devices in parallel for spatial neuromorphic memory.
why_it_matters: Direct optical write access to memristive arrays links sensing/imaging photonics with in-memory neuromorphic hardware and spatial data processing.
detailed_summary: The work combines a free-space 450 nm micro-LED array with two-terminal IGZO-rich/IGZO optoelectronic RRAM cells to program resistive states optically and electrically. It maps potentiation and depression versus pulse frequency, width, and amplitude, and demonstrates optical SET with electrical RESET. Persistent photocurrent is used as a fading-memory mechanism for temporal bit encoding, while multiple LED-to-ORRAM channels write spatial patterns across a chip.
platform_or_system: IGZO optoelectronic RRAM with micro-LED array
main_result: The authors demonstrate simultaneous spatial photonic programming of multiple IGZO ORRAM devices and hybrid optical SET/electrical RESET operation.
application_angle: The platform is relevant to optical-domain sensing and neuromorphic accelerators that need parallel, image-like memory programming.

title: Hundred-hertz quantum circuit iteration rate in a reusable neutral-atom array
abstract: Neutral-atom quantum processors have rapidly advanced in scale and coherence, yet their practical performance remains constrained by limited quantum circuit iteration rates (qCIRs) and information throughput. Here we experimentally demonstrate a high-throughput neutral-atom system based on non-destructive readout and atom reuse. By integrating a chip-based photonic interface with a 10-qubit array, we implement non-destructive readout with a retention probability of 99.7%, and further achieve a raw qCIR of 101Hz and a post-selected qCIR of 74.8Hz. More importantly, we verify a general throughput optimization methodology and obtain a normalized Fisher information rate of 57.7Hz, improving the achievable throughput by more than one order of magnitude compared with conventional methods. Our results establish a practical route toward high-throughput neutral-atom quantum processors.
one_liner: A reusable 10-qubit neutral-atom array reaches 101 Hz raw quantum-circuit iteration using nondestructive readout.
why_it_matters: Higher circuit repetition and atom reuse directly improve neutral-atom processor throughput, especially for sampling, metrology, and variational workloads.
detailed_summary: This experiment integrates a chip-based photonic interface with a 10-qubit neutral-atom array to perform nondestructive readout while retaining atoms with 99.7% probability. Reusing atoms after measurement yields a raw quantum circuit iteration rate of 101 Hz and a post-selected rate of 74.8 Hz. The authors also optimize throughput using normalized Fisher information rate, reaching 57.7 Hz and exceeding conventional operation by more than an order of magnitude.
main_result: The system achieves 101 Hz raw qCIR with 99.7% readout retention and demonstrates a 57.7 Hz normalized Fisher information rate.
application_angle: Fast iteration makes neutral-atom processors more practical for quantum algorithms, calibration loops, and sensing protocols limited by measurement throughput.

title: Classical-limit formula for matrix elements between bound states of distinct one-dimensional potentials
abstract: A classical-limit formula is derived for matrix elements between bound states of distinct one-dimensional potentials. We leave open the physical interpretation of the potentials, but generally envision them to be Born-Oppenheimer-type potentials with the position variable $x$ identifying with a slowly evolving degree of freedom of the system. For instance, $x$ could represent the internuclear separation in a diatomic molecule, with the potentials being potential energy curves for different electronic states. In this scenario, the matrix elements could be, e.g., conventional Franck-Condon factors. To test the derived formula, we assume functional forms for the potentials and operator that afford analytical solutions for the matrix elements. As the classical limit is approached, the computed matrix elements exhibit a clear tendency towards the classical-limit formula, providing strong validation for the formula. In future work, we anticipate using the formula to model inhomogeneous excitation spectra of atoms in one-dimensional optical lattices, with an eye towards improved optical lattice clock performance.
one_liner: A classical-limit expression is derived for bound-state matrix elements between distinct 1D potentials.
why_it_matters: The formula could simplify modeling of excitation spectra in optical lattices and help refine clock-system spectroscopy calculations.
detailed_summary: The paper derives a classical-limit formula for matrix elements connecting bound states of different one-dimensional potentials, motivated by Born-Oppenheimer potential curves. The authors test the expression using analytically solvable model potentials and operators, showing convergence toward the formula as the classical limit is approached. They identify future use in modeling inhomogeneous excitation spectra of atoms in one-dimensional optical lattices.
platform_or_system: 1D bound-state potentials and optical-lattice clock models
main_result: The authors provide and validate a classical-limit formula for transition matrix elements between bound states in distinct 1D potentials.
application_angle: More efficient spectral modeling can support improved optical lattice clock performance and interpretation of lattice-induced inhomogeneity.

title: Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation with Adversarial Errors
abstract: We prove a fault-tolerance theorem for quantum computation against adversarial noise. For every quantum circuit on $\bar{N}$ logical qudits of depth $\bar{T}$, we construct a fault-tolerant circuit on $N=\text{poly}(\bar{N})$ physical qudits of depth $\bar{T}\cdot\bar{N}^{o(1)}$, which is robust against an adversary who may arbitrarily choose and corrupt an almost-linear number $N^{1-o(1)}$ of physical qudits at each time step. This robustness significantly improves upon prior fault-tolerance theorems, which assumed corruptions were either local and stochastic, or else only act on a polynomially vanishing fraction of qudits. Our fault-tolerance scheme addresses a key bottleneck towards constructing quantum PCPs via the circuit-to-Hamiltonian mapping of Anshu, Breuckmann, and Nguyen (STOC'24). More fundamentally, our result demonstrates that fault-tolerant quantum computation remains possible under noise models that are global, worst-case, and non-Markovian over the full duration of the computation, directly countering concerns that correlated noise could fundamentally undermine quantum fault tolerance. Our construction is based on a new family of subsystem product codes we develop, which have large dimension and distance along with low-weight parity-checks, and which support transversal non-Clifford gates. We show how to perform single-shot fault-tolerant error correction on these codes using a Floquet-like procedure based on the local testability of classical tensor codes. We then obtain a universal fault-tolerance scheme using repeated code switching in a hypercubic qudit architecture. Finally, we recursively compose our scheme with itself to reduce an initially exponential qudit dimension down to a constant.
one_liner: A fault-tolerance theorem shows quantum computation can survive global, adversarial, non-Markovian qudit corruption.
why_it_matters: It strengthens the theoretical basis for scalable quantum hardware by addressing correlated worst-case noise beyond stochastic local models.
detailed_summary: The paper proves a fault-tolerance construction for logical qudit circuits under an adversary that corrupts an almost-linear number of physical qudits at each time step. The scheme uses new subsystem product codes with large dimension and distance, low-weight checks, and transversal non-Clifford gates. Single-shot error correction is implemented through a Floquet-like procedure based on classical tensor-code local testability, followed by code switching and recursive dimension reduction.
platform_or_system: fault-tolerant qudit architecture with subsystem product codes
main_result: The construction simulates any logical circuit with polynomial physical overhead and near-linear-depth overhead while tolerating global adversarial corruptions.
application_angle: Although theoretical, it informs hardware roadmaps by showing that severe correlated noise need not fundamentally rule out scalable fault tolerance.

title: Hydrodynamization in 1D Bose gases at nonzero temperature
abstract: Hydrodynamization refers to the remarkably rapid process in relativistic heavy-ion collisions by which hydrodynamic descriptions become applicable. Following the observation of analogous behavior in ultracold one-dimensional (1D) Bose gases, hydrodynamization has been conjectured to be a universal dynamical phenomenon in quantum systems following high-energy quenches. Theoretical studies in this cold-atom setting have so far been restricted to quenches from ground states. Here we study how nonzero temperatures affect hydrodynamization. Specifically, using a homogeneous 1D gas of hard-core bosons, we explore how the initial temperature affects the timescales associated with hydrodynamization and prethermalization following a Bragg-pulse quench. We find that while the hydrodynamization coherence time remains unchanged, increasing temperature shortens both the damping time of the hydrodynamization oscillations and the prethermalization time. We argue that this is mainly the result of the broadening of the initial rapidity distribution, and introduce a nonzero-temperature dephasing time defined in terms of the extent of the rapidity distribution.
one_liner: Finite temperature changes damping and prethermalization times after Bragg quenches in 1D hard-core Bose gases.
why_it_matters: Cold-atom hydrodynamization provides an experimentally controllable route to benchmark nonequilibrium quantum dynamics and thermalization models.
detailed_summary: The authors study hydrodynamization in a homogeneous one-dimensional hard-core Bose gas after a Bragg-pulse quench at nonzero initial temperature. They find that the hydrodynamization coherence time is temperature-insensitive, while higher temperature shortens both oscillation damping time and prethermalization time. The mechanism is attributed to broadening of the initial rapidity distribution, motivating a finite-temperature dephasing time.
main_result: Finite temperature leaves the coherence time largely unchanged but accelerates damping and prethermalization after the quench.
application_angle: The results guide cold-atom quantum simulators used to emulate transport, relaxation, and hydrodynamic emergence in many-body systems.

title: Astrophysical Graviton Squeezing Can Be Hidden in the Far-Field
abstract: While localized astrophysical sources can generate macroscopic graviton squeezing, their observable quantum signatures at far-field detectors remain unresolved. In this work, we investigate the propagation dynamics of the squeezed states using spatial quantum optics methods to evaluate correlation functions accessible to a local observer. Crucially, we reveal a severe kinematic conflict in same-cone measurements, which highly suppresses local quantum coherence. Consequently, these macroscopically squeezed states appear classically thermal to a single detector. Our results demonstrate that global squeezing does not guarantee local observability, and the measurable quantum signatures may be significantly weaker than what would be expected from the overall squeezing parameter of the state.
one_liner: Spatial quantum-optics analysis shows astrophysical graviton squeezing can look thermal to a far-field local detector.
why_it_matters: It clarifies what quantum signatures of gravity could actually be measurable, separating global squeezing from local detector observables.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes propagation of macroscopically squeezed graviton states from localized astrophysical sources using spatial quantum-optics correlation methods. It identifies a kinematic conflict in same-cone measurements that strongly suppresses locally accessible quantum coherence. As a result, a single far-field detector may see an effectively classical thermal signal despite large global squeezing.
main_result: The authors show that global astrophysical graviton squeezing can be hidden from local far-field observables.
application_angle: This constrains proposed quantum-gravity sensing strategies by emphasizing detector geometry and accessible correlation functions.

title: Multi-purpose quantum laboratories from superconducting circuits
abstract: Superconducting circuits (SCs) are the cornerstone of modern quantum technology, enabling scalable computing through coherent control of macroscopic quantum states. Through a legacy that predates modern quantum computing, SCs have emerged as high-precision instruments for discovery. In this review, we highlight the role of SCs as general-purpose quantum laboratories, outlining the emerging landscape of correlated matter-circuit science. We review and unify the capabilities of superconducting quantum hardware across condensed matter, high energy and quantum information sciences. We trace the technical evolution of these architectures, illustrating how their foundational development has culminated in a toolkit for resolving the complexities of macroscopic quantum states.
one_liner: Reviews superconducting circuits as general-purpose quantum laboratories for probing correlated macroscopic quantum states.
why_it_matters: Frames mature SC hardware as a discovery platform beyond computing, connecting precision control to condensed-matter, high-energy, and QI experiments.
detailed_summary: This review surveys superconducting circuits as controllable quantum systems for more than scalable computation. It emphasizes how coherent control, engineered coupling, and readout of macroscopic quantum states enable experiments across condensed matter, high-energy analogs, and quantum information science. The paper unifies hardware capabilities into a toolkit for resolving complex collective quantum behavior.
main_result: The main result is a synthesis of superconducting-circuit architectures as multi-purpose instruments for correlated matter-circuit science.
application_angle: The review highlights how existing quantum-computing hardware can be repurposed for precision simulation, sensing-adjacent measurements, and discovery experiments.

title: Hardware-Aware Compilation and Execution of Bivariate Bicycle Codes on Neutral-Atom Systems
abstract: Quantum computers are noisy; without quantum error correction (QEC), deep programs fail as qubits lose information due to decoherence. Among QEC approaches, bivariate bicycle (BB) codes offer low overhead and constant-depth syndrome extraction, while neutral-atom arrays provide scalable, reconfigurable qubit layouts. However, executing BB-code primitives on neutral-atom systems requires a hardware-aware mapping that respects movement, zoning, and interaction constraints. We present Park-n-Ride, a system for compiling and executing the BB code on neutral-atom processors. Park-n-Ride introduces a module layout and movement model aligned with neutral-atom constraints, exposes a compact BB-native logical interface for compilation, and integrates scheduling mechanisms that enable efficient execution on zoned architectures. By co-designing BB-code abstractions with hardware execution, Park-n-Ride provides a practical path from qLDPC primitives to resource-efficient, high-throughput execution on reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays.
one_liner: Introduces Park-n-Ride, a hardware-aware compiler for bivariate bicycle QEC codes on neutral-atom processors.
why_it_matters: It addresses the practical gap between qLDPC code primitives and executable schedules on zoned, movable, reconfigurable atom arrays.
detailed_summary: The paper presents Park-n-Ride, a compilation and execution system for bivariate bicycle codes on neutral-atom hardware. It defines module layouts, movement models, and scheduling mechanisms that respect constraints from atom transport, zoning, and interactions. The system exposes a compact BB-native logical interface to connect code-level primitives to hardware execution.
main_result: The main result is a hardware-aware execution framework for BB-code primitives on zoned neutral-atom processors.
application_angle: It supports more resource-efficient fault-tolerant execution by making low-overhead qLDPC codes more compatible with realistic neutral-atom machines.

title: Eigenframe Synchronization in Disordered Driven Quantum Ensembles
abstract: Periodic driving underlies many forms of quantum control, including spin-based quantum sensing. However, in an ensemble sensor, one waveform must act on spins with different detunings, drive amplitudes, hyperfine environments, and local fields. Existing robust-control approaches to such disorder are usually framed in terms of coherence, effective Hamiltonians, filter functions, or refocusing. Here we identify a complementary geometric requirement for collective ensemble Floquet control: disorder realizations must share a common Floquet eigenframe. When this condition is met, initialization, protection, signal coupling, and readout are defined in one dressed basis, so the ensemble responds as a collective Floquet sensor rather than as an average over inequivalent driven members. We make this condition measurable with an eigenvector-based synchronization order parameter and a complementary fragmentation metric that quantify the alignment and spread of Floquet quantization axes across the ensemble. As one realization of this framework, we use a continuous counterdiabatic Floquet drive to derive synchronization criteria and predict resonance-governed breakdown at the first two low-order commensurabilities between the engineered Floquet gap and the drive modulation, with detuning and amplitude disorder producing distinct breakdown channels. Experiments on a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) ensemble in diamond verify the synchronized regime through long-lived collective oscillations, a two-dimensional disorder-robustness map, and breakdown resonances that shift with the modulation rate. Finally, we demonstrate a harmonic-free continuous-drive AC magnetometry protocol whose collective single-tone response is enabled by the synchronized Floquet eigenframe. These results establish Floquet eigenframe synchronization as a measurable condition for disorder-resilient collective control and quantum sensing.
one_liner: Demonstrates Floquet eigenframe synchronization for disorder-resilient collective control in NV ensemble magnetometry.
why_it_matters: It gives ensemble sensors a measurable geometric control criterion, linking robust dressed-basis alignment to practical AC magnetic sensing.
detailed_summary: The work identifies common Floquet eigenframe alignment as a key condition for coherent ensemble control under detuning, amplitude, hyperfine, and local-field disorder. It defines an eigenvector synchronization order parameter and fragmentation metric to quantify whether disorder realizations share a dressed quantization axis. Experiments on NV ensembles verify long-lived collective oscillations, robustness maps, and resonance-governed breakdown, then use the synchronized regime for harmonic-free continuous-drive AC magnetometry.
main_result: The main result is experimental verification of Floquet eigenframe synchronization and its use in a single-tone continuous-drive AC magnetometry protocol.
application_angle: The framework can improve practical ensemble quantum sensors by making robust control and readout depend on a directly measurable synchronization condition.

title: Erbium-implanted tellurite waveguides with low-temperature post-implantation activation and signal enhancement
abstract: In this paper, we demonstrate erbium ion implantation and signal enhancement in tellurium oxide hybrid waveguides. Silicon nitride strips with a width of 2 $μ$m and a height of 100 nm were clad with a 110-nm-thick tellurium oxide layer to form hybrid waveguides, followed by erbium ion implantation at an energy of 200 keV and a dose of $1\times10^{15} ions/cm^{2}$, with a projected peak implantation depth of approximately 50 nm into the tellurium oxide layer. After low-temperature annealing at 150 °C for 30 minutes, the propagation loss decreased from 1.7 to 0.9 dB/cm, while the erbium lifetime increased from 40 $μ$m to over 800 $μ$m. We measure a small-signal enhancement of 9 dB in an 11-cm-long waveguide at a wavelength of 1550 nm. These results demonstrate progress towards a low-temperature post-ion implantation process for incorporating erbium and other rare earth ions into tellurium oxide films for integrated photonic applications.
one_liner: Shows erbium implantation and 1550 nm signal enhancement in tellurite hybrid waveguides after low-temperature annealing.
why_it_matters: Low-temperature rare-earth activation is important for integrating optical gain or active ions into backend-compatible photonic platforms.
detailed_summary: The paper demonstrates erbium ion implantation into tellurium oxide hybrid waveguides built from silicon nitride strips clad with a thin tellurium oxide layer. Implantation used 200 keV ions at a dose of 1e15 ions/cm2, with the peak placed about 50 nm into the tellurium oxide. A 150 C, 30 minute anneal reduced propagation loss from 1.7 to 0.9 dB/cm and produced a 9 dB small-signal enhancement at 1550 nm in an 11 cm waveguide.
main_result: The main result is 9 dB small-signal enhancement at 1550 nm after low-temperature post-implantation activation.
application_angle: The process is relevant for rare-earth-doped integrated amplifiers, light sources, and telecom-band photonic circuits compatible with temperature-sensitive stacks.

title: Local magnetic resonance of scalar spin chirality
abstract: Quantum states with finite scalar spin chirality carry an orbital magnetic moment that has eluded direct measurement. We show that a local drive breaks the cyclic symmetry and activates chirality-changing transitions. We propose two complementary probes: direct chirality resonance and chirality-resolved spin resonance. Lindblad simulations demonstrate their feasibility in locally addressable spin platforms, including scanning tunneling microscopy, silicon donors, and quantum dots.
one_liner: Proposes local resonance probes for detecting scalar spin chirality through chirality-changing transitions.
why_it_matters: It offers a route to access an orbital magnetic moment of chiral spin states that has been difficult to measure directly.
detailed_summary: The paper studies quantum states with finite scalar spin chirality and their associated orbital magnetic moment. It shows that a local drive can break cyclic symmetry and activate transitions that change chirality. The authors propose direct chirality resonance and chirality-resolved spin resonance, with Lindblad simulations indicating feasibility in locally addressable spin platforms.
main_result: The main result is a pair of proposed local magnetic-resonance protocols for resolving scalar spin chirality.
application_angle: These probes could enable nanoscale characterization of chiral magnetic states in STM, donor-spin, and quantum-dot platforms.

title: Exact Moments of Gaussian Gram Hafnians Reveal an $n^2/\log n$ Threshold for Weak Anticoncentration
abstract: Anticoncentration is central to hardness arguments for approximate sampling. In the independent Gaussian surrogate for collision free Gaussian boson sampling, the moment ratio studied here also determines the averaged ideal linear cross entropy reference value. Let $H_{k,n}=\mathrm{haf}(X^{\mathsf T}X)$, where $X\in\mathbb{C}^{k\times 2n}$ has independent standard circular complex Gaussian entries. We evaluate $\mathbb{E}|H_{k,n}|^2$ and $\mathbb{E}|H_{k,n}|^4$ exactly by reducing four hafnian copies to a rank two Gaussian integral. For $R_{k,n}=(\mathbb{E}|H_{k,n}|^2)^2/\mathbb{E}|H_{k,n}|^4$, we obtain $R_{k,n}=4^{-n}\binom{2n}{n}/F_{k,n}$, where $F_{k,n}={}3F_2(-n,-n,1/2;1,k/2;1)$ is a terminating generalized hypergeometric polynomial. If $k/n^2\to c>0$, then $F{k,n}\to e^{1/c}I_0(1/c)$, where $I_0$ is the modified Bessel function of the first kind of order zero, and consequently $R_{k,n}\sqrt{πn}\to[e^{1/c}I_0(1/c)]^{-1}$. Thus $k\asymp n^2$ is a smooth Bessel crossover, whereas the scaling order boundary for inverse polynomial weak anticoncentration is $k\asymp n^2/\log n$. These conclusions concern the Gaussian surrogate moment criterion; finite dimensional Haar moment transfer and high probability small ball anticoncentration remain separate problems.
one_liner: Derives exact Gaussian Gram hafnian moments and an n^2/log n weak-anticoncentration threshold for a GBS surrogate.
why_it_matters: It sharpens sampling-hardness diagnostics for Gaussian boson sampling by separating surrogate moment criteria from harder Haar and small-ball questions.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes the independent Gaussian surrogate for collision-free Gaussian boson sampling using hafnians of Gaussian Gram matrices. It exactly evaluates second and fourth moments by reducing four hafnian copies to a rank-two Gaussian integral. The resulting moment ratio shows a smooth Bessel crossover at k proportional to n^2 and an inverse-polynomial weak-anticoncentration boundary at k proportional to n^2/log n, while noting that Haar transfer and high-probability small-ball results remain separate.
main_result: The main result is an exact moment formula giving an n^2/log n scaling boundary for weak anticoncentration in the surrogate criterion.
application_angle: The result informs how photonic sampling experiments and complexity arguments should interpret mode-number scaling and anticoncentration evidence.

title: Lie-Algebraic Classical Simulation of Bosonic Systems Beyond Gaussian Dynamics
abstract: Classical simulability is ultimately determined by both the dynamics of a quantum system and the observables being evaluated. Lie-algebraic simulation exploits the latter to make exact polynomial-time classical simulations by propagating observables through low-dimensional invariant operator spaces. However, its conventional formulation in terms of polynomial-dimensional dynamical Lie algebras does not directly accommodate bosonic systems as their algebras are neither compact nor semisimple. In this contribution, we overcome this limitation, making bosonic systems accessible to the Lie-algebraic programme of exact polynomial-time classical simulation. We prove that expectation values, fixed-order correlation functions, including multi-time correlators and out-of-time-ordered correlators, and gradients are efficiently computable whenever their operator modules have polynomial dimension. This recovers Gaussian quantum optics and extends it to non-Gaussian input states, while identifying exact polynomial regimes of interacting non-Gaussian dynamics including bounded-photon Kerr and pair-hopping Hamiltonians and nilpotent polynomial phase dynamics. We show that unlike in the finite-dimensional spin and fermionic setting treated previously, a finite-dimensional bosonic generator algebra alone does not guarantee finite observable dynamics. We further derive a controlled perturbative hierarchy for squeezing beyond exact sector confinement and confirm the predicted error orders numerically. We also evaluate operator spreading on interacting chains of up to $400$ modes and connect a topological doublon band with flux-reversed edge motion. These results provide a unified formalism for classifying, discovering, and systematically approximating tractable bosonic quantum dynamics with classical polynomial-time simulation.
one_liner: Extends exact Lie-algebraic simulation to bosonic systems with non-Gaussian states and selected interacting dynamics.
why_it_matters: It sharpens the boundary between useful bosonic quantum advantage and classically tractable photonic or oscillator dynamics.
detailed_summary: The paper generalizes Lie-algebraic classical simulation to bosonic systems whose generator algebras are noncompact or nonsemisimple. It proves efficient computation of expectation values, fixed-order and multi-time correlators, OTOCs, and gradients when the relevant operator modules remain polynomial-dimensional. The framework recovers Gaussian optics while adding exact tractable regimes for non-Gaussian inputs, bounded-photon Kerr, pair hopping, and nilpotent polynomial phase dynamics.
main_result: The work identifies exact polynomial-time simulation regimes for broad bosonic dynamics beyond Gaussian quantum optics.
application_angle: It gives photonic hardware designers a concrete test for when proposed non-Gaussian circuits may still be efficiently classically simulated.

title: Hardness of approximation for minimum-weight decoding of two-dimensional topological quantum codes
abstract: Efficient decoding is essential for the practical realization of fault-tolerant quantum computers. We study the computational complexity of minimum-weight decoding for topological quantum codes. For surface codes under the depolarizing channel, we consider Minimum-Weight decoding, which seeks a minimum-weight Pauli error consistent with both the $X$- and $Z$-syndromes. For color codes under independent $X$- and $Z$-error models, we consider Separate Minimum-Weight decoding. Assuming $P\neq NP$, we establish polynomial additive inapproximability gaps for these problems. Specifically, for the toric code and the $4.8.8$ color code on the torus, there exists a constant $c>0$ such that no polynomial-time algorithm can always produce a solution whose weight is within $cN^{1/14}$ of the optimum, where $N$ is the number of qubits, unless $P=NP$. For the planar surface code, we obtain an $Ω(N^{1/18})$ gap. Our inapproximability results use Håstad's hardness of approximation for MAX-3SAT. Our reduction develops a general, modular framework for embedding logical constraints into coupled primal--dual join problems on a lattice. A key ingredient is a localization argument that controls unintended interactions between different parts of the construction.
one_liner: Proves polynomial additive inapproximability for minimum-weight decoding in surface and color topological codes.
why_it_matters: Decoder limits directly affect fault-tolerant quantum hardware roadmaps and clarify which optimal-decoding goals are computationally unrealistic.
detailed_summary: The paper studies minimum-weight decoding for toric and planar surface codes under depolarizing noise and separate minimum-weight decoding for 4.8.8 color codes. Assuming P is not NP, it proves polynomial additive gaps, including cN^(1/14) for toric and color-code cases and Omega(N^(1/18)) for planar surface codes. The reduction embeds logical constraints into coupled primal-dual join problems on a lattice with a localization argument controlling unintended interactions.
main_result: It establishes that no polynomial-time algorithm can always approximate optimal decoding within the stated polynomial additive gaps unless P equals NP.
application_angle: The result motivates practical decoders that optimize reliability and speed rather than chasing exact minimum-weight solutions.

title: Block Encoding Non-Abelian Lattice Gauge Theory
abstract: Gauge theories like lattice QCD present a complex problem for quantum simulation. In a basis where the electric part of the Hamiltonian is simple, the magnetic part, generally expressed as a sum over the plaquette operators of the lattice, is quite complicated, producing correlated transitions between several link and site degrees of freedom. We provide an efficient block encoding of the plaquette operator in the irrep basis, a refinement of the electric basis where the internal gauge-variant degrees of freedom are integrated out. The construction removes the plaquette matrix element scaling wall which has been a significant barrier for other approaches in this basis. The algorithm leverages a convenient factorization property of the matrix elements, cheap classical precomputation, and quantum oracles built from lookup tables and programmed rotations.
one_liner: Presents an efficient block encoding of non-Abelian lattice-gauge plaquette operators in the irrep basis.
why_it_matters: Efficient plaquette access is a core bottleneck for quantum simulation of lattice QCD-like non-Abelian gauge theories.
detailed_summary: The work constructs an efficient block encoding for the plaquette operator in the irreducible-representation basis, where electric terms are simple but magnetic terms are usually costly. It uses factorized matrix elements, inexpensive classical precomputation, and quantum lookup-table oracles with programmed rotations. The approach targets the matrix-element scaling wall that has limited irrep-basis simulations.
platform_or_system: digital quantum simulation of non-Abelian lattice gauge theory
main_result: The paper gives an efficient block-encoding algorithm for plaquette dynamics after integrating out internal gauge-variant degrees of freedom.
application_angle: It improves the algorithmic path toward resource-feasible quantum simulations of lattice QCD and related gauge-theory models.

title: Entanglement assisted quantum $(r,δ)$-locally recoverable codes
abstract: Quantum $(r,δ)$-locally recoverable codes are quantum error-correcting codes capable of correcting $δ-1$ qudit erasures within one subset of qudits of cardinality at most $r+δ-1$. In this paper, we introduce the more general framework of entanglement-assisted quantum $(r,δ)$-locally recoverable codes, assuming that the local recovery operation is assisted by receiver-held qudits that remain unaffected by erasures. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for these codes to satisfy this property. For codes derived from Hermitian or Euclidean constructions, we establish connections between entanglement-assisted quantum and classical notions of $(r,δ)$-local recoverability, and derive a Singleton-like bound. Furthermore, we construct optimal pure entan\-gle\-ment-assisted quantum $(r,δ)$-locally recoverable codes from several families of classical codes, including bivariate $J$-affine variety codes, BCH codes, and homothetic-BCH codes.
one_liner: Introduces entanglement-assisted quantum locally recoverable codes and constructs optimal pure code families.
why_it_matters: Local erasure recovery with receiver-side entanglement could reduce repair overhead in quantum memories and networks.
detailed_summary: The paper defines entanglement-assisted quantum (r,delta)-locally recoverable codes, where receiver-held qudits assist local recovery from erasures. It gives necessary and sufficient conditions for the property and connects Hermitian and Euclidean constructions to classical local recoverability. It also derives a Singleton-like bound and constructs optimal pure codes from affine-variety, BCH, and homothetic-BCH code families.
